speaker: Carson Block
title: Carson Block: Building Muddy Waters, Short Selling, Quant Strategies & Market Risk
question: From an after-tax wealth-building perspective, why is active short selling structurally disadvantaged compared to buying and holding broad equity index ETFs?
guest: Look at our numbers as fund managers: we put up good numbers. But the taxation on active trading or short selling is all short-term capital gains taxation, so we pay ordinary income rates. When I was in California, I was paying like 52 or 53 percent. Compare that to a long-term capital gain: even if you realize that once a year, it is a little north of 20 percent, and it had been 17.5 percent for a while. And if you just own an ETF, you do not have to realize that gain at all, so it can compound untaxed. The best part is that if you have enough money in that ETF, a private bank will lend you money against it, so you can effectively live off the appreciation without ever having a taxable event.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Short selling fights three structural headwinds that a buy-and-hold index investor has working in their favor instead.

First, taxes. Under U.S. rules, gains on short sales are almost always treated as short-term capital gains, taxed at ordinary income rates, no matter how long the position stays open. An index ETF holder defers tax indefinitely, pays lower long-term rates on eventual sale, and may avoid the gain entirely through a step-up in basis at death. Deferral lets the untaxed gains keep compounding.

Second, expected return. Equities carry a positive risk premium, so a short seller is betting against long-run upward drift. Their payoff is also asymmetric: gains are capped at 100% while losses are theoretically unlimited, and a winning short shrinks as a share of the portfolio rather than compounding.

Third, carrying costs. Shorts pay stock borrow fees and margin interest, and must reimburse dividends to the lender. Those payments in lieu are deductible only as investment interest if you itemize and hold the short open more than 45 days. Short sellers also face margin calls and forced buy-ins, and frequent trading adds transaction costs. Index ETFs, by contrast, have minimal fees, low turnover, and qualified dividend treatment.

models.answer:
Active short selling faces severe tax, cost, and return headwinds that compound against long-term wealth accumulation. Under U.S. tax rules, short-sale profits are generally taxed at higher short-term capital gains (ordinary income) rates regardless of holding period, and active turnover repeatedly realizes annual tax drag. Conversely, broad equity index ETFs use in-kind redemptions to avoid capital gains distributions, letting unrealized wealth compound tax-deferred for decades before facing lower long-term capital gains rates—or escaping income tax entirely via a step-up in basis at death—while distributing mostly lower-taxed qualified dividends. 

Beyond taxes, short sellers fight the positive long-run equity risk premium while enduring inverted payoff asymmetry: maximum gains are capped at 100% and require continual taxable reinvestment to compound, whereas losses are theoretically unlimited, inviting margin calls and forced covering at unfavorable prices during rallies. Finally, while index ETF holders collect dividends and pay negligible expense ratios, short sellers owe ongoing stock-borrow fees, trading friction, and cash payments in lieu of dividends (which face strict investment-interest deductibility limits), steadily eroding net after-tax returns.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
Short selling loses on taxes, on costs and on the shape of its returns, while a buy-and-hold index ETF gets the best treatment on each.

On taxes, U.S. rules generally treat short-sale gains as short-term no matter how long the position is open (IRC §1233). That means they're taxed at ordinary income rates of up to 37%, while long-term gains are taxed at 15–20%. You can't defer tax indefinitely either, because borrow fees and margin make holding a short costly. A long position, by contrast, compounds untaxed until you sell and gets a step-up in basis at death. The payments you make to the lender in place of dividends usually can't be deducted, or only in limited ways. Index ETFs pay mostly qualified dividends and rarely distribute capital gains, because in-kind redemptions let them shed low-basis shares without tax.

On costs, a short pays borrow fees, margin interest and those dividend payments, all of which are ongoing drags.

On returns, stocks drift upward over time, so a short fights the equity risk premium. The most a short can make is 100%, but its losses have no ceiling. A winning short also shrinks, while a winning long grows and compounds.

Active short selling usually realizes gains when positions are closed, and those gains are typically taxed at short-term rates. Frequent trading accelerates the tax bill, while stock-borrow fees and payments in lieu of dividends reduce returns.

A short can be profitable, but it has to overcome those costs and the market’s upward drift to build wealth as effectively after tax.

Active short selling fights the stock market’s long-run upward trend and adds costs that compound against you. You pay stock-borrow fees, reimburse the lender for dividends, and may have to close a position at a loss if it triggers a margin call. The most you can earn on a short is the stock’s initial price, while losses can exceed that amount.

In a U.S. taxable account, profitable stock shorts are typically taxed at short-term rates, and closing them regularly can create a recurring tax bill. A broad equity index ETF generally has low fees and limited capital gains distributions. You can defer tax on price appreciation until you sell, and gains on shares held for more than a year generally qualify for lower long-term rates. That deferral leaves more money invested and compounding, while the ETF gives you diversified exposure to the market’s long-run growth.
